{{Short description|Mathematical operation}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Zak transform'''<ref name=EM/><ref name=TAH/> (also known as the '''[[Israel Gelfand|Gelfand]] mapping''') is a certain operation which takes as input a function of one variable and produces as output a function of two variables. The output function is called the Zak transform of the input function. The transform is defined as an [[infinite series]] in which each term is a product of a [[Dilation (affine geometry)|dilation]] of a [[Translation (geometry)|translation]] by an [[integer]] of the function and an [[exponential function]].  In applications of Zak transform to [[signal processing]] the input function represents a [[Signal (electrical engineering)|signal]] and the transform will be a mixed [[time]]–[[frequency]] representation of the signal. The signal may be [[real number|real valued]] or [[Complex number|complex-valued]], defined on a continuous set (for example, the real numbers) or a [[discrete set]] (for example, the integers or a finite subset of integers). The Zak transform is a generalization of the [[discrete Fourier transform]].<ref name=EM>{{eom|Zak transform}}</ref><ref name=TAH>{{cite book|editor=Alexander D. Poularikas|title=Transforms and Applications Handbook|date=2010|publisher=CRC Press|isbn=978-1-4200-6652-4|pages=16.1–16.21|edition=3rd}}</ref>

The Zak transform had been discovered by several people in different fields and was called by different names. It was called the "Gelfand mapping" because [[Israel Gelfand]] introduced it in his work on [[eigenfunction]] expansions. The transform was rediscovered independently by [[Joshua Zak]] in 1967 who called it the "k-q representation". There seems to be a general consensus among experts in the field to call it the Zak transform, since Zak was the first to systematically study that transform in a more general setting and recognize its usefulness.<ref name=EM/><ref name=TAH/>

==Continuous-time Zak transform: Definition==
In defining the continuous-time Zak transform, the input function is a [[function of a real variable]]. So, let ''f''(''t'') be a function of a real variable ''t''. The continuous-time Zak transform of ''f''(''t'') is a function of two real variables one of which is ''t''. The other variable may be denoted by ''w''. The continuous-time Zak transform  has been defined variously.

===Definition 1===

Let ''a'' be a positive constant.  The Zak transform of ''f''(''t''), denoted by ''Z''<sub>''a''</sub>[''f''], is a function of ''t'' and ''w'' defined by<ref name=EM/>
:<math>Z_a[f](t,w) = \sqrt{a}\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}f(at + ak)e^{-2\pi kw i}</math>.

===Definition 2===

The special case of Definition 1 obtained by taking ''a'' = 1 is sometimes taken as the definition of the Zak transform.<ref name=TAH/> In this special case, the Zak transform of ''f''(''t'') is denoted by ''Z''[''f''].
:<math>Z[f](t,w) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}f(t + k)e^{-2\pi kw i}</math>.

===Definition 3===

The notation ''Z''[''f''] is used to  denote another form of the Zak transform. In this form, the Zak transform of ''f''(''t'') is defined as follows:
:<math>Z[f](t,\nu) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}f(t + k)e^{-k\nu  i}</math>.

===Definition 4===

Let ''T'' be a positive constant. The Zak transform of ''f''(''t''), denoted by ''Z''<sub>''T''</sub>[''f''], is a function of ''t'' and ''w'' defined by<ref name=TAH/>
:<math>Z_T[f](t,w) = \sqrt{T}\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}f(t + kT)e^{-2\pi kwT i}</math>.
Here ''t'' and ''w'' are assumed to satisfy the conditions 0 ≤ ''t'' ≤ ''T'' and 0 ≤ ''w'' ≤ 1/''T''.

==Example==
The Zak transform of the function
:<math>\phi(t)=\begin{cases}1,&0\le t<1 \\ 0, &\text{otherwise}\end{cases}</math>
is given by
:<math>Z[\phi](t,w)=e^{-2\pi \lceil -t\rceil w i}</math>
where <math>\lceil - t\rceil </math> denotes the smallest integer not less than <math>-t</math> (the [[ceiling function]]).

==Properties of the Zak transform==
In the following it will be assumed that the Zak transform is as given in Definition 2.

'''1. Linearity'''

Let ''a'' and ''b'' be any real or complex numbers. Then
:<math>Z[af+bg](t,w)=aZ[f](t,w)+bZ[g](t,w)</math>
'''2. Periodicity'''

:<math>Z[f](t, w+1) = Z[f](t,w)</math>
'''3. Quasi-periodicity'''
:<math>Z[f](t+1, w)= e^{2\pi w i}Z[f](t,w)</math>
'''4. Conjugation'''
:<math> Z[\bar{f}](t,w)=\overline{Z[f]}(t,-w)</math>
'''5. Symmetry'''

:If ''f''(''t'') is even then <math>Z[f](t,w)=Z[f](-t,-w)</math>

:If ''f''(''t'') is odd then <math>Z[f](t,w)= -Z[f](-t,-w)</math>
'''6. Convolution'''

Let <math> \star</math> denote [[convolution]] with respect to the variable ''t''.
:<math>Z[f\star g](t,w)=Z[f](t,w)\star Z[g](t,w)</math>

==Inversion formula==
Given the Zak transform of a function, the function can be reconstructed using the following formula:
:<math>f(t)= \int_0^1 Z[f](t,w)\, dw.</math>

==Discrete Zak transform: Definition==
Let <math>f(n)</math> be a function of an integer variable <math>n \in \mathbb Z</math> (a [[sequence]]). The discrete Zak transform of <math>f(n)</math> is a function of two real variables, one of which is the integer variable <math>n</math>. The other variable is a real variable which may be denoted by <math>w</math>. The discrete Zak transform  has also been defined variously. However, only one of the definitions is given below.

===Definition===

The discrete Zak transform of the function <math>f(n)</math> where <math>n</math> is an integer variable, denoted by <math>Z[f]</math>, is defined by 
:<math>Z[f](n,w)=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} f(n+k)e^{-2\pi k w i}.</math>

===Inversion formula===

Given the discrete transform of a function <math>f(n)</math>, the function can be reconstructed using the following formula:
:<math>f(n)= \int_0^1 Z[f](n,w)\, dw.</math>

==Applications==
The Zak transform has been successfully used in physics in [[quantum field theory]],<ref>{{cite book|last1=J. Klauder, B.S. Skagerstam|title=Coherent States|publisher=World Scientific|date=1985}}</ref> in electrical engineering in [[Time–frequency representation|time-frequency representation]] of signals, and in digital data transmission. The Zak transform has also applications  in mathematics. For example, it has been used in the Gabor representation problem.
